caption_en:
1932: The Palestine Post was Jewish. 📰 The story of a name that changed owners.

Before 1948, "Palestine" was on the letterhead of Jewish institutions:
• The Palestine Post, founded 1 Dec 1932 by Gershon Agron, became The Jerusalem Post in 1950.
• The Anglo-Palestine Company (1902, a Zionist movement bank) became Bank Leumi le-Israel in 1951.
• The Palestine Orchestra (first concert 26 Dec 1936, Toscanini conducting) became the Israel Philharmonic in 1948.
• Mandatory Palestine's team in the 1934 World Cup qualifiers vs Egypt fielded only Jewish players; after 1948 it became Israel's national team.
• Under the Palestinian Citizenship Order (1925), Jews and Arabs alike were Palestinian citizens until 1948. Photo: the 1935 passport of a Jewish worker from Petah Tikva.

Arabs used the name too: Filastin, an Arabic daily, was founded in Jaffa in 1911. Historians such as Rashid Khalidi (Palestinian Identity, 1997) trace Palestinian Arab identity to the late Ottoman and early Mandate years; it grew much stronger after 1948 and 1967.

The flag: the Arab Revolt flag (1916 to 1918), in pan-Arab colours, used in Mandate Palestine from the 1920s, adopted by the All-Palestine Government in Gaza (Oct 1948) and by the PLO, the Palestine Liberation Organization, founded 28 May 1964 in East Jerusalem, then under Jordan. Jordan's flag is almost identical, plus a seven-pointed star; Sudan, Kuwait and the UAE use the same four colours.
The PLO's first chairman was Ahmad Shukeiri, not Yasser Arafat. Arafat co-founded Fatah in the late 1950s and became PLO chairman in 1969.

Every nation is born at some point: Jordan in 1946, Israel in 1948. Today millions call themselves Palestinian, and that's real. The name just has a surprising history.

Sources: The Jerusalem Post archives; JTA (1950); Bank Leumi history; Palestinian Citizenship Order (1925); RSSSF and FIFA records (1934); Israel Philharmonic Orchestra and Britannica; Palestinian Journeys, Institute for Palestine Studies (Filastin, PLO); Rashid Khalidi, Palestinian Identity (1997); Flags of the World; Britannica (Arafat, PLO, Jordan).
Photos, Wikimedia Commons: The Palestine Post 16 May 1948; Zoltan Kluger, GPO 1938; Government of Mandatory Palestine passport 1935; Palestine Orchestra 1936; Rudi Weissenstein 1948; Arab Revolt 1916 to 1918; Ahmad Shukeiri 1965 (all public domain); Filastin 1936 (CC BY-SA 4.0). 1932: הפלסטיין פוסט היה עיתון יהודי. 📰 הסיפור של שם שהחליף בעלים.
לפני 1948 "פלשתינה" הופיע על מוסדות יהודיים: הפלסטיין פוסט (מ־1950 הג'רוזלם פוסט), תזמורת פלשתינה (מ־1948 הפילהרמונית הישראלית), בנק אנגלו־פלשתינה (מ־1951 בנק לאומי), ונבחרת פלשתינה ב־1934 שכל שחקניה יהודים. בתקופת המנדט יהודים וערבים כאחד היו אזרחים פלשתינאים. גם ערבים השתמשו בשם: העיתון "פלסטין" יצא ביפו מ־1911.
הדגל? דגל המרד הערבי מ־1916. ממשלת כל פלסטין בעזה אימצה אותו ב־1948, ואש"ף, שנוסד ב־1964 במזרח ירושלים תחת שלטון ירדן, אימץ אותו גם. היו"ר הראשון של אש"ף: אחמד שוקיירי. ערפאת נכנס רק ב־1969.
כל אומה נולדת מתישהו: ירדן ב־1946, ישראל ב־1948. היום מיליונים מגדירים את עצמם פלסטינים, וזה אמיתי. לשם פשוט יש היסטוריה מפתיעה.

lines.line: Nineteen thirty-two: the Palestine Post, a Jewish newspaper.
Watch the word Palestinian change owners.
Nineteen oh two: the Anglo-Palestine Bank, founded by Zionists.
Under the British, Jews and Arabs were Palestinian citizens.
Thirty-four: Palestine's World Cup team, every player Jewish.
Thirty-six: the Palestine Orchestra, Jewish musicians.
Arabs used the name too: the Jaffa paper Filastin.
Nineteen forty-eight, Israel is born. Rebrand time.
The Palestine Post becomes The Jerusalem Post.
The orchestra: Israel Philharmonic. The bank: Bank Leumi. The team: Israel.
Palestinian now means the Arabs of the land.
The flag? Older than you think.
Nineteen sixteen, the Arab Revolt flag.
Forty-eight, Gaza's All-Palestine Government adopts it.
Sixty-four, the PLO, the Palestine Liberation Organization, takes it.
Jordan's flag? Almost identical, plus a star.
First leader? Not Arafat, but Ahmad Shukeiri.
Every nation is born sometime: Jordan forty-six, Israel forty-eight.
Today millions call themselves Palestinian, and that's real.
The name has a surprising history. It started with a newspaper.
